source.title: Fusion Power Module Market to Reach USD 11.79 Billion by 2034 as Data Center Power Infrastructure Demand Accelerates
source.body:
Global Fusion Power Module Market was estimated at USD 5,000.00 million in 2025 and is projected to reach USD 5,500.00 million in 2026. According to Energy Resources Insights, the market could reach USD 11,789.74 million by 2034, representing an analyst-derived compound annual growth rate (CAGR) of 10.0% during 2026–2034. Market development is associated with increasing requirements for integrated electrical infrastructure in hyperscale data centers, cloud computing facilities and colocation environments. The expansion of high-density computing infrastructure is creating opportunities for factory-assembled power modules that simplify electrical integration and deployment.

Fusion power modules, as defined in this report, are factory-assembled and tested electrical power-distribution solutions designed for data center infrastructure. They can combine transformer interfaces, switchgear, uninterruptible power supply (UPS) equipment, batteries, protection systems, monitoring and controls. These solutions are supplied through integrated power skids, electrical distribution houses and containerized power modules. The market definition does not refer to nuclear fusion equipment and excludes standalone UPS systems, independent switchboards, batteries sold separately, cooling-only modules, server racks and complete data halls.
Market at a Glance
•	2025 market size: USD 5,000.00 million
•	2026 estimate: USD 5,500.00 million
•	2034 forecast: USD 11,789.74 million
•	Forecast CAGR: 10.0% during 2026–2034
•	Leading regional market: Asia-Pacific
•	Leading application category: Hyperscale and cloud data centers
•	Key architectures: Integrated UPS and distribution modules, electrical distribution E-Houses and modular power skids
Data Center Expansion Supports Demand for Integrated Power Modules
The growing scale and complexity of data center infrastructure are creating demand for reliable and efficiently integrated electrical distribution solutions. Hyperscale computing facilities, cloud platforms and colocation operators require coordinated power infrastructure to support continuous operations and increasing electricity requirements.
Traditional electrical infrastructure projects often involve multiple suppliers, separately procured components and extensive on-site integration. Factory-assembled power modules provide an alternative by combining several electrical functions into standardized assemblies. This approach can shift integration and testing activities away from construction sites, potentially reducing installation complexity and supporting more predictable project execution.
The development of artificial intelligence and high-performance computing is adding further pressure to data center electrical infrastructure. Higher power densities increase the importance of equipment coordination, protection, power quality and system monitoring. Integrated power modules can help operators organize electrical distribution around the requirements of modern computing facilities.
The International Energy Agency identifies approximately USD 500 billion in global data center investment for 2024. This broader investment figure provides an important industry reference, although it includes many assets beyond the specific integrated power modules covered in this report.

Key Market Drivers and Challenges
Several factors are shaping the industry's outlook:
•	Hyperscale data center expansion: New computing facilities require coordinated electrical distribution and reliable power infrastructure.
•	Artificial intelligence infrastructure: High-density computing increases the need for carefully designed power systems and integrated electrical equipment.
•	Factory-based assembly: Pre-engineered modules can shift integration and testing away from congested construction sites.
•	Standardized electrical infrastructure: Modular designs support repeatable configurations and can simplify procurement and commissioning.
•	Infrastructure modernization: Expansion and retrofit projects create opportunities to replace or upgrade existing electrical distribution arrangements.
The market also faces challenges. High initial capital expenditure can affect procurement decisions, particularly for projects with complex electrical requirements. Integration with existing infrastructure, equipment compatibility, safety standards and commissioning procedures require careful planning. Furthermore, suppliers may provide individual components without offering complete integrated assemblies, making the market boundary important when assessing actual module revenue.
Segmentation and Regional Outlook
The market is segmented by architecture, cooling configuration, customer category and deployment type.
•	Architecture: Integrated UPS and distribution module, electrical distribution E-House and modular power skid.
•	Cooling configuration: Air-cooled independent and liquid-assisted integrated.
•	Customer: Hyperscale and cloud, colocation, enterprise and edge.
•	Deployment: Greenfield facility, expansion and retrofit.
Asia-Pacific is identified as the leading regional market. Growing digital infrastructure investment, cloud computing requirements and data center development provide opportunities for integrated electrical equipment suppliers. North America and Europe also represent important markets because of their established data center ecosystems and continued investment in computing infrastructure.
Regional demand depends on electricity availability, construction activity, power reliability requirements, equipment procurement practices and the ability of suppliers to deliver integrated solutions. The adoption of modular infrastructure is also influenced by project size, site conditions and commissioning schedules.
Competitive Landscape
The competitive environment includes electrical equipment manufacturers, power distribution specialists, UPS suppliers and data center infrastructure solution providers. Companies compete through system integration capabilities, equipment reliability, manufacturing capacity, engineering expertise and delivery timelines.
Eaton's NordicEPOD specifications demonstrate commercially available integrated electrical module configurations in the 1.7–3.1 MW range. A Siemens–Compass announcement concerning electrical solution manufacturing capacity also illustrates the industrial development of modular data center power infrastructure. These examples demonstrate product and manufacturing activity rather than establishing global market shares or annual delivery volumes.
Competitive positioning increasingly depends on the ability to provide factory-tested assemblies that coordinate power distribution, protection, backup and monitoring functions. Suppliers capable of supporting large-scale data center projects and repeatable deployment requirements may benefit from the continued development of modular electrical infrastructure.
